definition: The part of a database that turns an ordinary optimisable SQL query into results through parsing, analysis, rewriting, planning and execution. PostgreSQL utility commands can take other paths.
The first stage of query processing. It checks that the SQL text follows the grammar and builds a parse tree; it does not yet know whether tables or columns exist.
example: A typo such as SELEC fails in the parser with "syntax error at or near".

definition: A tree-shaped representation of a SQL statement built by the parser, with one node per piece of grammar (the SELECT list, the FROM clause and so on).
The query-processing stage that looks every table, column and function name up in the system catalog, checks types and produces a query tree. "Column does not exist" errors come from here.
PostgreSQL's internal form of a statement after analysis: a tree in which every name has been resolved to a real table, column or function. The rewriter and planner work on it.
The query-processing stage that applies rewrite rules to the query tree before planning. Its main job is view expansion; row-level security conditions are also added at this point.
Replacing a reference to an ordinary view with the view's defining query, so the planner can optimise the combined query as one.
example: SELECT * FROM pending_orders WHERE customer_id = 42 becomes a query on orders with both conditions, so an index on customer_id can be used.

definition: The query-processing stage that runs the chosen plan, calling each plan operator in turn and streaming result rows back to the client.
The shape of a query plan: a tree whose nodes are operators such as scans, joins and sorts. Rows flow from the leaves (usually table scans) up to the root, which produces the result.
example: Limit -> Sort -> HashAggregate -> Hash Join, with two Seq Scans as the leaves.

definition: One step in a query plan. A logical operator says what is computed (read a table, join, group); a physical operator is the specific algorithm chosen for it (Seq Scan or Index Scan, Hash Join or Merge Join).
example: The logical "join" in a query may become a Nested Loop, Hash Join or Merge Join in the plan.

definition: An optimisation that moves a filter condition as far down the plan tree as possible, usually into the table scan, so that later operators such as joins process fewer rows. The movement is valid only when it preserves semantics, especially for outer joins and NULLs.
example: Filtering orders on status inside the scan means the join sees 30,066 rows instead of 1,000,000.

definition: Online transaction processing: many relatively small queries and changes, such as placing orders or fetching individual customers. The balance of planning and execution costs depends on the workload.
A query that scans and aggregates large amounts of data, such as a report over billions of rows, rather than fetching a few rows. Such workloads are often called OLAP (online analytical processing).

The classic way plan operators pass rows: every operator offers open(), next() and close(), and each parent calls next() on its child to pull one row at a time. Named after Goetz Graefe's Volcano system (around 1990).
example: A Limit that has its two rows stops calling next(), so the scan below it does no more work.

definition: A Python function containing yield, which produces values one at a time when asked and pauses in between. It behaves like an operator in the iterator model.
A database that stores each row's columns together on a page, which suits reading and writing whole rows. PostgreSQL and MySQL are row stores.
An execution model that processes batches of values between operators, amortising per-tuple overhead and enabling efficient loops. It is separate from parallel execution and columnar storage.

Compiling operations into native code before or during execution rather than interpreting every operation. Query engines can fuse several operators into a loop; PostgreSQL JIT instead compiles expressions and tuple-deforming work, rather than an entire fused plan.
PostgreSQL can compile expressions and tuple-deforming work to machine code at runtime using LLVM. Compilation has an initial cost, so whether it helps depends on how much work follows.
An open-source compiler toolkit that turns an intermediate code representation into machine code for many processors. PostgreSQL uses it for JIT compilation.
PostgreSQL can split a plan across several worker processes, for example each scanning part of a table (Parallel Seq Scan), and combine their results in a Gather node.
Running a query in a single process with no parallel workers. In PostgreSQL, setting max_parallel_workers_per_gather = 0 forces it, which makes plans simpler to read.
A PostgreSQL plan node that starts parallel worker processes and collects the rows they produce into a single stream.
An open-source columnar database for analytical queries over very large datasets, using vectorised execution.
A research database from TU Munich (Thomas Neumann's group) that showed how to compile whole query plans into fast machine code, described in a 2011 VLDB paper.
A research database from TU Munich, the successor to HyPer, which also compiles plans to machine code.
A commercial distributed SQL database (formerly MemSQL) that compiles queries to machine code.
MySQL's default storage engine. It stores tables in 16 KiB pages by default.
Very Large Data Bases: one of the main international research conferences on databases.
A Python web framework with its own ORM. Its select_related (a join) and prefetch_related (additional batched queries) options load related rows eagerly to avoid N+1 queries.
A Python database toolkit and ORM. Its selectinload and joinedload options load related rows eagerly to avoid N+1 queries.
A web tool that takes the text or JSON output of EXPLAIN ANALYZE and shows each node's exclusive time and misestimates, which makes long plans easier to read.
Solid-state drive: storage using semiconductor memory rather than moving disks. Its latency and throughput depend on the device and workload; the name alone does not determine page-read latency.
A hard disk drive stores data on rotating platters. Seeking to unrelated locations adds mechanical work; PostgreSQL cost parameters can model a difference between random and sequential access.
Operating system: the software (such as Linux) that manages the hardware. PostgreSQL asks it for file pages, and it keeps its own cache of recently read file data.
Input/output: reading data from or writing data to storage. Query cost analyses count page I/Os, where reading or writing one page counts as one.
example: Reading a 1,000-page table once is 1,000 page I/Os.

definition: Reading pages in their stored order, often allowing storage and the operating system to read ahead. PostgreSQL models sequential page fetches with seq_page_cost, default 1.0; actual access cost depends on storage and cache state.
Reading pages in an order unrelated to how they are stored, as an index scan does when it fetches scattered rows. PostgreSQL charges random_page_cost (default 4.0) per such page.
A unit of data equal to 1,024 bytes. PostgreSQL pages are normally 8 KiB.
A unit of data equal to 1,024 KiB, or 1,048,576 bytes.
A unit of data equal to 1,024 MiB, or 1,073,741,824 bytes.
example: 10 GiB of 8 KiB pages is 1,310,720 pages.

definition: Units of data. In PostgreSQL settings and EXPLAIN output, kB means 1,024 bytes and MB means 1,024 kB, so they equal KiB and MiB.
example: work_mem = 4MB is 4,096 kB.

definition: A thousandth of a second. EXPLAIN ANALYZE reports times in milliseconds.
A millionth of a second, or one thousandth of a millisecond. It is a unit of time, not a guaranteed duration for a memory or storage access.
A fixed-size block used to store database data. PostgreSQL normally uses eight-kibibyte blocks, selected at build time; touching a page can involve memory caches or physical storage.

PostgreSQL’s main table storage, holding physical row versions in pages without a guaranteed logical row order. Standard builds use 8 KiB pages; page size is selected at build time. An ordinary index scan visits heap rows, while a suitable index-only scan can skip a heap visibility check when the page is marked all-visible.

One stored version of a logical row. PostgreSQL MVCC can retain older versions after an UPDATE so transactions with older snapshots can still see them; VACUUM later reclaims versions no active snapshot can need.
PostgreSQL's cache of database blocks in memory shared by database sessions. A buffer hit avoids an OS read request for that block; a miss can still be served from the OS page cache.

An EXPLAIN option that reports how many pages each node touched: shared hit, shared read, dirtied, written and temp read/written. Since PostgreSQL 18 it is on by default with ANALYZE. Counts are totals across all loops.
example: Buffers: shared hit=7011 read=342 means 7,353 page accesses.

definition: A page access that found the page already in PostgreSQL's shared buffers, so no request to the operating system was needed.
A page PostgreSQL had to request from the operating system because it was not in shared buffers. It may still come from the OS page cache, so it is not necessarily a disk read.
In EXPLAIN BUFFERS output, dirtied counts pages the query modified in shared buffers; written counts pages it had to write out itself to free space.

Temporary files are scratch files a program writes to disk and removes when it is done. PostgreSQL writes them when a sort or hash does not fit in its memory limit, and EXPLAIN's temp read / written counts the pages it read from and wrote to them.
example: Buffers: temp read=2421 written=2421 shows a hash join that spilled.

definition: Memory in which the operating system keeps recently read file data. A PostgreSQL "read" that hits it is served from memory, not disk.
A warm cache already holds useful data; a cold cache has little of it. These descriptions are relative to a workload and cache layer: restarting PostgreSQL need not empty the operating system cache.
A PostgreSQL setting that records time spent in I/O calls for reads and writes. Those calls can be served by the operating system cache, so the timing does not isolate physical device time.

Flags PostgreSQL sets on a row the first time it checks whether the row's transaction committed, so later readers need not check again. Setting them dirties pages, so even a read-only query can write.

The Oversized-Attribute Storage Technique: PostgreSQL can compress large column values or store them out of line in a separate table. Fetching or decompressing those values can be deferred until an operation needs their contents.

The formulas an optimiser uses to turn estimated row and page counts into a cost for each operator. PostgreSQL charges per page read, per row and per operator evaluated, using settings such as seq_page_cost.
The arbitrary units used for PostgreSQL planner costs. The default sequential page cost is 1.0, and cost settings can be changed; the units are not milliseconds.
example: cost=0.00..19853.00 means a total of 19,853 units.

definition: The first number in EXPLAIN's cost=a..b: the estimated work before a node can return its first row. Blocking operators such as Sort have a high startup cost.
The cost of all the work, added up. In PostgreSQL's EXPLAIN output it is the second number in cost=a..b: the estimated work to return all of a node's rows, including its children.
PostgreSQL's cost for reading one page in sequence, default 1.0. All other cost settings are relative to it.
PostgreSQL's relative planner charge for a non-sequential page fetch, default 4.0 in version 18. Choosing another value should reflect measured storage and cache behaviour across the workload.
PostgreSQL's cost for processing one row, default 0.01.
PostgreSQL's cost for processing one index entry during an index scan, default 0.005.
PostgreSQL's cost for evaluating one operator or function call, such as a comparison in a WHERE clause, default 0.0025.
A PostgreSQL setting that tells the planner roughly how much memory is available for caching data (shared buffers plus OS cache). It changes cost estimates only; it allocates nothing.
The textbook way of comparing join and sort algorithms by counting page reads and writes, ignoring CPU work and the cost of writing the final result.
A PostgreSQL command that collects statistics for planning, usually by sampling large tables. Within EXPLAIN, ANALYZE instead means execute the statement and report actual execution figures.

PostgreSQL background maintenance that can VACUUM and ANALYZE eligible tables. Analysis thresholds and periodic scheduling do not promise an immediate run; temporary tables require manual maintenance.

A PostgreSQL setting controlling the detail of column statistics. For standard scalar analysis, target 100 requests 30,000 sample rows on a large table; other analysers and the available rows can alter sampling.
A PostgreSQL system view showing the column statistics ANALYZE collected: null_frac, n_distinct, most_common_vals, most_common_freqs, histogram_bounds and correlation.
The PostgreSQL catalog table describing tables and indexes. Its reltuples and relpages columns hold the estimated row and page counts from the last VACUUM or ANALYZE.
example: Reading reltuples gives an instant approximate row count.

definition: In pg_stats, the fraction of a column's rows that are NULL.
In pg_stats, the estimated number of distinct values in a column. A negative value means a fraction of the row count, so -1 means every row is different, as for a primary key.
example: n_distinct = 91709 for orders.customer_id.

definition: The list of a column's most frequent values and the fraction of rows holding each (most_common_vals and most_common_freqs in pg_stats). The planner uses the stored frequency directly for those values.
example: If pending has frequency 0.030767, WHERE status = 'pending' is estimated at 30,767 of 1,000,000 rows.

definition: A list of values (histogram_bounds) that divides a column's non-MCV values into buckets holding equal numbers of rows. The planner estimates range conditions by counting buckets and interpolating within one.
example: With 100 buckets, a value 8⅓ buckets from the top gives a selectivity of about 8.3%.

definition: In pg_stats, a number between minus one and one describing how physical heap order relates to a column's sorted order. A magnitude near one tends to place nearby index keys on nearby heap pages; near zero, matching rows can be scattered. The number of matching pages still depends on selectivity.
example: orders.id has correlation 1.0 because ids were inserted in order.

definition: Predicting how many rows an operation will produce, using statistics and selectivity rules. Errors can affect access paths, join algorithms and join order.
A difference between an estimated and actual row count. Large errors are worth investigating from the leaves upwards; tenfold is a diagnostic heuristic rather than a universal failure threshold.
Treating filter conditions as unrelated when combining selectivities. Multiplication estimates their conjunction under independence; dependence can produce overestimates or underestimates.
Columns whose values are statistically related. Suitable extended statistics can improve estimates for supported conditions, but do not fix every kind of dependency or join estimate.

Statistics on expressions or combinations of columns collected through CREATE STATISTICS. PostgreSQL 18 supports functional dependencies, distinct-combination counts and multivariate most-common-value lists, with different uses and limitations.
Planner statistics that no longer describe the table, typically after a bulk load and before the next ANALYZE. They are a leading cause of bad row estimates.
How an optimiser chooses which candidate plans to cost. PostgreSQL uses dynamic programming over join orders for smaller joins and GEQO for very large ones.
The sequence and tree shape in which a plan joins its inputs. Legal reordering depends on the join types and predicates; different choices can produce very different intermediate row counts.
A left-deep join tree joins one base table at a time to the result so far; a bushy tree may join two intermediate results. Counting both shapes gives far more possible plans.
example: 10 tables have 3,628,800 left-deep orders but over 17 billion trees of any shape.

definition: One way of reading a table that the planner considers: a sequential scan, an index scan on a particular index, or a bitmap scan. Planner 'paths' are also partial plans for joins.
A sort order that may help a later step, such as a merge join or ORDER BY. The planner keeps a costlier path that produces one, because it may avoid a sort later.

PostgreSQL's genetic query optimiser, used by default once a query has 12 or more FROM items (geqo_threshold). It searches join orders with a genetic algorithm and finds a good plan, not necessarily the best, in reasonable time.
A PostgreSQL setting (default 8) that limits how many explicit JOIN items are flattened into one list for the planner to reorder.
Examining every candidate in a defined search space. Join planning commonly uses pruning and restrictions to avoid enumerating every full physical plan.

Examining successive data locations or records in order. PostgreSQL’s Seq Scan visits table pages and checks visible tuples against its filter; a full scan visits the whole relation, but a parent such as LIMIT can stop it early.
A scan that answers the query from the index alone, without fetching rows from the heap, when every needed column is in the index and the page is marked all-visible in the visibility map.

A two-step scan: a Bitmap Index Scan collects the locations of all matches into an in-memory bitmap, then a Bitmap Heap Scan reads those heap pages in physical order. A middle ground between an index scan and a seq scan.
Plan nodes combining tuple-location bitmaps from index scans. BitmapAnd intersects locations and BitmapOr unites them; lossy page entries require tuple rechecks in the heap scan.

Lossy bitmap pages retain page locations rather than individual tuple locations, so the heap scan must recheck candidate rows. Memory pressure can cause lossification, while some index methods are inherently lossy; a displayed Recheck Cond alone does not prove either cause.

A query-plan condition evaluated by an index access method. Leading B-tree bounds can narrow a contiguous search; later-key conditions may instead reject index entries without reducing that range. A separate Filter is applied after access.

EXPLAIN ANALYZE output counting rows rejected by a filter, averaged across loops when there are several executions. Large rejection counts suggest checking whether a more selective access path would help.

Accesses to physical row versions in PostgreSQL table storage. On an Index Only Scan, EXPLAIN’s Heap Fetches field counts heap visibility checks still required when a page is not marked all-visible. Updates can clear visibility bits and older snapshots can delay all-visible marking; VACUUM may help when visibility permits.
An EXPLAIN ANALYZE field added in PostgreSQL 18: how many times a node walked down from the index root to a leaf. Normally 1 per loop; skip scans can make many.
example: Index Searches: 1031 means 1,031 separate descents.

definition: Reading a contiguous run of index entries between two bounds, which a B-tree can do because its entries are sorted.
example: WHERE created_at >= '2026-03-01' AND created_at < '2026-03-02' is one range scan.

definition: The order in which rows actually sit in the table's pages. If it follows a column (high correlation), rows matching a range of that column are packed onto few pages.
The two inputs of a join. In a PostgreSQL plan the first child is the outer and the second the inner; a nested loop re-runs the inner side once per outer row.
The two inputs of a hash join. The build side (under the Hash node, usually the smaller input) is loaded into a hash table; the probe side streams past and each row looks up matches.
The column or columns compared in a join's condition, such as orders.customer_id = customers.id.
A physical way of computing a join. PostgreSQL has three: nested loop, hash join and merge join.
A nested-loop join that uses a parameterised index lookup for its inner input. It can be attractive for a small outer input; caching, duplicates, visibility and match count affect its cost.
A nested loop that loads as much of the outer table into memory as fits (a block) and scans the inner table once per block instead of once per row.
example: 1,000 outer pages in blocks of 100 means 10 scans of the inner table.

definition: In textbook join and sort costing, the number of page-sized memory slots an algorithm may use, usually written B.

PostgreSQL's hash join when the build side exceeds its memory budget: both inputs are split into batches by hashing the join key, one batch stays in memory and the rest go to temporary files and are joined one by one.

A textbook hash join that partitions both inputs to disk and then joins matching partition pairs in memory. The usual three-I/O-per-page model assumes one partitioning level, build partitions fitting in memory, and excludes final output writes.
The slots of a hash table. EXPLAIN shows Buckets; PostgreSQL sizes them automatically. A collision is two keys landing in the same bucket.
Sorting data bigger than memory: pass 0 sorts memory-sized chunks and writes them out as sorted runs, then each later pass merges many runs into one. EXPLAIN shows it as Sort Method: external merge.
example: With 102 buffer pages, a 1,000-page table sorts in 2 passes.

definition: A chunk of data written out in sorted order during an external merge sort, later merged with other runs.

PostgreSQL plan names describe the physical join orientation and preservation of unmatched rows. Hash Right Join can result from swapping a SQL LEFT JOIN; Hash Right Anti Join instead returns unmatched rows from its right input.
A PostgreSQL plan node (since version 14) above a nested loop's inner side that caches results by join key, so repeated keys are served from memory. EXPLAIN ANALYZE shows its Hits and Misses.
The function that rounds a number up to the next whole number, written ⌈x⌉. ⌈2.1⌉ = 3 and ⌈3⌉ = 3.

The inverse of raising to a power: the logarithm to base b of x is the power you must raise b to in order to get x, so log₂(1,024) = 10 because 2^10 = 1,024. It grows very slowly, which is why B-trees are shallow.
n! means 1 × 2 × … × n, the number of ways to order n items. It grows explosively: 10! = 3,628,800.
The number of child pointers in an internal B-tree page. Capacity, actual occupancy, key width and leaf capacity determine height; a high branching factor can keep paths shallow.

Ordering values or rows by a comparison key. A PostgreSQL Sort node orders its input; a full Sort reads all input before returning rows, while Incremental Sort can complete already-presorted groups separately.
An in-memory comparison-sorting algorithm. PostgreSQL EXPLAIN can report quicksort for full sorts that fit memory; bounded top-N and external sorts use other methods.
A bounded sorting method that retains the best requested rows while inspecting every input row. PostgreSQL may use it for ORDER BY with LIMIT; small inputs or other paths can use other methods.
A PostgreSQL plan node that completes a sort when the input is already sorted on a leading part of the key, sorting only within each group.
A plan operator that must read all its input before it can return any row, such as Sort, a hash join's Hash build or HashAggregate. A LIMIT above it cannot stop the work below.
A plan operator that passes rows on as soon as it produces them, such as a scan, a filter or the probe side of a hash join.

The PostgreSQL command that shows the plan chosen for a statement with its estimates. EXPLAIN ANALYZE also runs the statement and adds actual rows, times, loops and buffers, so it really changes data for INSERT, UPDATE or DELETE.
An EXPLAIN option that adds each node's output column list and schema-qualified names.
An EXPLAIN option that lists planner-related settings changed from their defaults, which helps when reading someone else's plan.
An EXPLAIN option that prints the plan as machine-readable JSON, as used by plan visualisers.
An EXPLAIN ANALYZE option that keeps actual row counts but skips per-node timing, whose clock calls add overhead on some systems.
An EXPLAIN ANALYZE option added in PostgreSQL 17 that also measures the cost of converting result rows to their output format.

In EXPLAIN ANALYZE each node shows the planner's estimate (rows= in the first brackets) and what happened (actual rows, an average per loop). loops says how many times the node ran; multiply per-loop figures by it.
example: rows=3.00 loops=200 means 600 rows in total.

definition: In EXPLAIN ANALYZE, actual time=a..b gives the milliseconds to a node's first and last row, per loop and including its children. Planning Time and Execution Time are totals for the whole statement.
In EXPLAIN, the estimated average size of a node's output rows in bytes.

Inclusive node time includes child execution. For a simple serial plan, subtracting child totals from a parent total approximates its own work after accounting for loops; parallel execution and instrumentation make subtraction less direct.
A PostgreSQL module that automatically logs the plans of statements slower than a threshold you set.
A PostgreSQL extension that records, per query shape, how often it ran (calls) and its total and mean execution time, so you can find the queries that cost most overall.
One key in an index together with a pointer to the row (or rows) holding it. B-tree leaf pages hold the entries in sorted order.
A CREATE INDEX clause that stores extra columns in the leaf entries without making them part of the key, so they are not sorted but can serve index-only scans.
example: CREATE INDEX ON orders (customer_id) INCLUDE (ordered_on, total).

definition: A per-heap-page map with two bits: all-visible and all-frozen. VACUUM sets these conservatively; changes clear them. An index-only scan can skip heap visibility checks when the all-visible bit is set.
Wasted space in tables and indexes from dead row versions and free space that has not been reclaimed, which makes scans read more pages.

A collation using C-locale ordering rather than language-specific sorting rules. For text pattern searches, PostgreSQL can use a normal B-tree under C ordering or a suitable pattern operator class under other supported collations.
An index (via the pg_trgm extension, using GIN or GiST) on every three-character sequence of a text value, which lets PostgreSQL search for substrings such as LIKE '%abc'.
Generalized Search Tree: a flexible PostgreSQL index type used for geometric data, ranges and trigram search.
Searching documents by words rather than exact strings, with stemming and ranking; PostgreSQL provides it with tsvector, tsquery and GIN indexes.

Block Range Index: a PostgreSQL index storing summaries, such as value ranges, for groups of heap pages. It is a summarising index; changing a column referenced only by such indexes does not by itself prevent a HOT update.
A PostgreSQL index type that supports only equality lookups, with no ordering or ranges.

A PostgreSQL B-tree optimisation that can combine equal keys into posting-list entries containing multiple tuple locations. Applicability depends on operator classes and index properties; INCLUDE indexes do not use deduplication.
Extra storage writes caused by a logical change. Maintaining applicable indexes and write-ahead-log records can add work; HOT and partial-index predicates affect which maintenance is required.
An index whose lookups another index already serves, such as one on (customer_id) next to one on (customer_id, ordered_on). It costs writes and cache space for little gain.

PostgreSQL statistics views: pg_stat_user_indexes counts scans per index (idx_scan), and pg_stat_user_tables counts updates (n_tup_upd) and HOT updates (n_tup_hot_upd). Counts are per server and reset with stats resets.
A copy of the database kept up to date from the primary server, often used to serve read queries. Its index usage statistics are kept separately from the primary's.
The PostgreSQL command that rebuilds an index. Its CONCURRENTLY form permits ordinary reads and writes during much of the operation but still uses locks and can wait for transactions.

A workload-dependent index design guideline: use leading equality keys, then keys that serve ordering or range restrictions. A selective range before an ordering column can require a sort, so compare alternatives with actual plans.

Describes a predicate that supplies useful search conditions for the chosen index. Bare indexed-column comparisons often qualify; a function may need a matching expression index. Not every index scan is a selective search.

A difference between a value’s type and the type an operation expects. A language or protocol may reject it, convert the value, or treat it as unknown data. In PostgreSQL comparisons, a cast on an indexed column can remove a useful search bound, while supported cross-type operators can still use the index.
A quoted SQL literal initially having the unknown type. PostgreSQL often resolves it to the comparison column's type; the final type depends on surrounding operator-resolution rules.
A LIKE pattern starting with %, such as '%abc'. Matches can begin with anything, so no ordinary B-tree can narrow the search; a trigram index can.

Pagination that skips a specified number of preceding results before returning a page. Computing skipped results can add substantial work; PostgreSQL exposes this through LIMIT and OFFSET, while actual latency depends on the plan, filters and cache state.
example: OFFSET 900000 walked 900,020 index entries to return 20 rows.

definition: Object-relational mapper: a library that maps database rows to objects in application code and generates the SQL, such as Django's ORM or SQLAlchemy.
Loading related rows up front with a join or one batched query, instead of one query per object when each is first used (lazy loading).
A record of the steps, including each database call, made while handling one request. It reveals N+1 patterns that no single EXPLAIN shows.
A statement parsed and analysed once (PREPARE) and then run many times with different parameter values (EXECUTE), which can reuse a cached plan.

A prepared-statement plan generated using that execution's parameter values. With PostgreSQL 18 plan_cache_mode set to auto, the first five parameterised executions normally use custom plans before generic-plan comparison.

A prepared-statement plan generated without execution-specific parameter values. PostgreSQL can reuse it when its estimated cost compares favourably with custom plans and planning overhead; reuse on the sixth execution is not guaranteed.
A PostgreSQL setting choosing between custom and generic plans for prepared statements; force_custom_plan always plans with the real values.
A placeholder such as $1 in a SQL statement, filled with a value at execution time. Drivers send parameter values separately from the SQL text.
count(*) over a whole table. Under MVCC different transactions can see different rows, so PostgreSQL keeps no stored total and must scan a table or index to count.
Extract, transform, load: a batch process that copies data from sources, reshapes it and loads it into a database.
A separate system used to test changes before deploying them to production. A staging table instead holds data during a load or transformation; these are distinct meanings of staging.
Comma-separated values: a plain-text format with comma-separated fields. Records are normally separated by line breaks, but quoted fields may themselves contain commas, quotes or line breaks.
The data a workload accesses regularly. When it exceeds available cache capacity, more requests may reach lower cache layers or storage; the access distribution also matters.

A form of PostgreSQL's VACUUM that rewrites the whole table into a new file without dead row versions, giving the space back to the operating system. It holds an exclusive lock for the whole rewrite, so the table can't be read or written meanwhile.
A PostgreSQL B-tree scan walking keys in reverse order. It can supply descending order when the key order, equality constraints and NULL ordering match the query.

The textbook nested loop join that scans the whole inner table once for every outer row. In page I/Os it costs M + |R| × N, where M and N are the two tables' page counts and |R| is the outer row count.

The textbook name for a merge join whose inputs must first be sorted on the join key, usually by an external merge sort. Counted in page I/Os, it costs about 5 I/Os per page of both tables with two-pass sorts, or 3 if the final merge pass feeds the join directly.

A PostgreSQL plan node that computes GROUP BY results from input already sorted by the group key, finishing each group when the key changes. HashAggregate is the alternative that needs no sorted input.
A join condition other than equality. A pure inequality join needs a nested loop in PostgreSQL 18; a join with an additional suitable equality clause can use hash or merge plus a residual condition.
A tree or graph of physical operations chosen to compute a query. Scans supply rows to joins, grouping and sorting operators; the chosen plan depends on estimates and available paths.
A page-sized memory location available to a textbook join or sort algorithm. This teaching model counts memory in page slots and differs from an EXPLAIN buffer-access counter.

A PostgreSQL B-tree operator class that compares text character by character for pattern operations. It can support prefix LIKE searches when locale-sensitive ordering would not supply the required bounds.
A condition checked on candidate row pairs in a PostgreSQL join. It differs from a scan filter, and its interaction with preserved unmatched rows depends on whether the join is outer.

Extended planner statistics estimating whether one column value determines another. PostgreSQL applies them to supported equality and constant-IN restrictions, with limitations; they do not model every correlation.
Extracting individual column values from PostgreSQL's stored row representation into values an executor expression can use. JIT compilation can accelerate this work as well as expression evaluation.

A PostgreSQL plan node that retains rows from a child so they can be read again, for example on the inner side of a nested loop. It can fill lazily as rows are requested; retained rows can spill to temporary files when the memory budget is exceeded.

Combining rows into intermediate group summaries before a later query operation. It can reduce work only when regrouping the summaries preserves the intended result; partial averages need both sums and counts, and joins can multiply summaries.

Finding candidate table rows through an index using one or more search keys. PostgreSQL may still need heap visits to retrieve columns or check row visibility, and an index lookup can return several matching rows.

An execution model where a query operator sends produced rows or batches to downstream operators, rather than waiting for a parent to request each row. Snowflake’s 2016 design paper describes this model alongside columnar and vectorised execution.

Work that keeps an index consistent with table changes and reclaims obsolete entries. INSERT and relevant non-HOT UPDATE operations can add entries; partial indexes hold only rows satisfying their predicate, HOT can avoid new ordinary index entries, and obsolete entries may be reclaimed later, for example by VACUUM. Summarising indexes such as BRIN have their own maintenance rules.
example: Changing an INCLUDE value in a B-tree can prevent HOT and require new ordinary index entries. Inserting a row outside a partial index’s predicate adds no entry to that index.
